citation.authors: Rekhter, Y.; Moskowitz, B.; Karrenberg, D.; de Groot, G. J.; Lear, E.
citation.title: Address Allocation for Private Internets (RFC 1918, BCP 5)

claims.quote: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has reserved the following three blocks of the IP address space for private internets: 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 (10/8 prefix) 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 (172.16/12 prefix) 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 (192.168/16 prefix)

claims.finding: RFC 6890 (which obsoletes RFC 5735) registers 127.0.0.0/8 as "Loopback" (Forwardable: False, Global: False; defined in RFC 1122 s3.2.1.3) and 169.254.0.0/16 as "Link Local" (RFC 3927; Forwardable: False, Global: False). The whole /8 is loopback, not just 127.0.0.1.
claims.quote: Address Block | 127.0.0.0/8 | Name | Loopback | RFC | [RFC1122], Section 3.2.1.3 ... Address Block | 169.254.0.0/16 | Name | Link Local | RFC | [RFC3927]
claims.location: RFC 6890 section 2.2.2, Table 4 (Loopback) and Table 5 (Link Local)

claims.planned: CIDR prefix notation: /n = n leading network bits; a /24 has 256 addresses
claims.finding: RFC 4632 s3.1: prefix = 4-octet quantity, "/", then a decimal 0-32 giving the number of significant (most significant, network) bits. Its table lists /24 = 256 addresses, /16 = 65536, /12 = 1048576, /8 = 16777216, /32 = 1 ("host route"), 0.0.0.0/0 = 4294967296 ("default route"). The RFC counts addresses in the block; it does NOT state the folklore "254 usable hosts" figure - do not attribute that to this RFC.
claims.quote: In CIDR notation, a prefix is shown as a 4-octet quantity, just like a traditional IPv4 address or network number, followed by the "/" (slash) character, followed by a decimal value between 0 and 32 that describes the number of significant bits.
claims.location: RFC 4632 section 3.1, Basic Concept and Prefix Notation

extra_findings.finding: Worked example of what /16 and /24 mean as masks.
extra_findings.quote: the legacy "Class C" network number 192.168.99.0 is defined as the prefix 192.168.99.0/24; the most significant 24 bits are ones and the least significant 8 bits are zeros.

extra_findings.finding: CIDR size table rows useful for a page: /32 1 address "host route"; /24 256; /16 65536; /12 1048576; /8 16777216; 0.0.0.0/0 4294967296 "default route".

extra_findings.quote: Forwarding in the Internet is done on a longest-match basis.
extra_findings.location: RFC 4632 section 5.1, Rules for Route Advertisement

extra_findings.finding: Private addresses are not routed on the public Internet: routes and packets for them should be filtered between enterprises/ISPs. This is why a container with a 172.17.x.x address needs NAT to reach the Internet.
extra_findings.quote: Because private addresses have no global meaning, routing information about private networks shall not be propagated on inter-enterprise links, and packets with private source or destination addresses should not be forwarded across such links.

extra_findings.finding: Private space can be used without coordinating with IANA or a registry, so the same addresses are reused in many places (unambiguous only within one enterprise).
extra_findings.quote: An enterprise that decides to use IP addresses out of the address space defined in this document can do so without any coordination with IANA or an Internet registry.

extra_findings.finding: RFC 1918 names the blocks "24-bit block" (10/8), "20-bit block" (172.16/12 = 16 contiguous class B networks) and "16-bit block" (192.168/16 = 256 contiguous class C networks).
extra_findings.quote: the first block is nothing but a single class A network number, while the second block is a set of 16 contiguous class B network numbers, and third block is a set of 256 contiguous class C network numbers.

extra_findings.finding: Loopback addresses must never appear on the wire.
extra_findings.quote: Internal host loopback address. Addresses of this form MUST NOT appear outside a host.

extra_findings.finding: Link-local 169.254/16 is only valid on the directly connected link and routers must not forward it - which is why the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254 is only reachable from the instance itself / its link.
extra_findings.quote: A router MUST NOT forward a packet with an IPv4 Link-Local source or destination address, irrespective of the router's default route configuration or routes obtained from dynamic routing protocols.

extra_findings.finding: RFC 3927 purpose: auto-configured addresses in 169.254/16 valid only for same-link communication; self-assigned addresses are chosen from 169.254.1.0-169.254.254.255 (first and last 256 addresses reserved).
extra_findings.quote: it selects an address using a pseudo-random number generator with a uniform distribution in the range from 169.254.1.0 to 169.254.254.255 inclusive.

extra_findings.finding: 100.64.0.0/10 is "Shared Address Space" for carrier-grade NAT (RFC 6598); not RFC 1918 private space but likewise not globally routable (Global: False in RFC 6890 Table 3).
extra_findings.quote: The Shared Address Space address range is 100.64.0.0/10.

extra_findings.finding: RFC 6890 obsoletes RFC 5735 (and 4773, 5156, 5736); cite 6890 for the special-purpose registry. In its tables all three RFC 1918 blocks are "Private-Use", Forwardable True, Global False.

Documentation-only blocks safe for examples in course pages: 192.0.2.0/24 (TEST-NET-1), 198.51.100.0/24 (TEST-NET-2), 203.0.113.0/24 (TEST-NET-3). 0.0.0.0/8 is "This host on this network"; 255.255.255.255/32 limited broadcast; 240.0.0.0/4 reserved.

teaching_notes: Authoritative for the exact private ranges (note 172.16/12 stops at 172.31.255.255 - agents and humans routinely misjudge 172.x addresses). RFC 5735 listed in sources.json is obsolete: cite RFC 6890. RFC 4632 gives the address-count table but never the "usable hosts = 2^n - 2" folklore; if a page wants 254, it must say it is convention (network + broadcast address), not cite this RFC. Docker default bridge 172.17.0.0/16 sits inside the 172.16/12 block (executed evidence in the netfilter and dns notes).
